patterns: is a schoolteacher a specific job
entries.answer: A teacher is someone whose work is helping other people learn, and the word is defined by that activity rather than by any qualification. Tutor, lecturer and instructor each name a part of the same job at a different level, and schoolteacher in British usage specifically teaches young children. The word has since widened to anyone who instructs at all, which is why a tour guide teaches as well and nobody finds that odd.

entries.answer: A student is a person who studies, and the word does not imply a school age, since university students are the largest group in most countries. That is a real difference from a pupil, which in British English does specify a child in school. Outside education the word widened further, so the students of a master means people studying under that person, and older writing uses it for anyone being taught anything at all.

entries.answer: A classroom is the room where teaching happens, and the word is a compound that simply marks the purpose of the space rather than anything about its shape or size. The awkward modern usage is classrooms standing for the teaching itself, as in classrooms across the country are underfunded, where no room is involved. An older sense of a teaching group survives in the phrase, which still means a class as well as a room.

entries.answer: An assignment is a piece of work set to somebody, and the word is used at school, at university and at work for that same idea at different weights. At school it is routine and dated, and at work it usually means a particular project with a deadline attached. An older academic sense meaning an appointment to a post survives in the phrase, and in practice the two senses never meet.

entries.answer: An exam is a formal test of knowledge, and in British English the full word examination is written out while in American usage the short form is normal for both. It differs from a test in standing, since an exam is graded and certificated while a test is a smaller check on one topic. The term quiz came in much later for a short informal check, and revision is the study done beforehand while review is the check afterwards.

entries.answer: A semester is one half of an academic year, and it belongs to the American system, while British and Commonwealth institutions use a term, which can run to three a year or only two, and the two words are not interchangeable in practice. Inside a semester there are usually teaching weeks followed by reading weeks with no classes at all. The word comes from a Latin term meaning six months, though a semester is nearer four or five, so the name overstates it.
